text: I signed up for a garment-making class right when the cold weather settled in, and I have been meaning to tell you how it is going. Our teacher opened the first session by passing around scraps of fabric and asking us to hem a cotton square by hand. My stitches wandered off in every direction, crooked and uneven. I pulled them all out and started over, two evenings running. At the next session she showed us how to baste, a loose row of stitches that holds the layers still so nothing slides under the needle. It looks like pointless extra work until the day you skip it. After that came mending. I patched a worn trouser knee with a heavier piece of canvas, stitched on from underneath. Yesterday I finished a lined skirt. I am coming home with a box of pins, a metal thimble and every intention of keeping at it.

units: the little balls on a knit come from the length of the filaments

text: So what makes a sweater start pilling after barely a handful of washes? The answer comes down to the length of the fibers themselves. The short ones work their way to the surface, tangle together under friction and roll into the little balls that make a garment look tired. A long fiber spun into a tightly twisted yarn holds up much better, because the loose ends stay trapped inside the strand. Then a cheap sweater is doomed? Usually, yes, although the cut of the garment and the way you care for it count just as much. A sleeve that rubs against a bag strap all day will pill no matter how good the knit is. Can you fix it? Of course. A fabric shaver or a fine comb lifts the top layer right off. The operation does lighten the color a little, so work slowly and stop well before you have gone too far.

text: The man who runs the alterations workshop remembers a customer who walked in one morning with a coat whose lining was falling apart under the arms. “She was sure it was finished,” he says. He sees the same thing constantly. The lining is cut from a light cloth, and it gives out long before the wool around it, because it takes all the rubbing from the shoulder. Setting the whole thing right takes a single session at the machine. He opens the armhole, swaps the ruined panel for fresh satin in the same shade, then closes the seam by hand so no ridge shows through. “That coat has another ten years in it,” he adds. He turns away any job that would cost more than buying a replacement. His book is full three weeks out, which tells him that people are turning back toward repair. Bring it in, he says, at the first loose stitch.

text: Getting a clear, steady color out of cloth once demanded a kind of patience we no longer have. The dye came from pounded roots, boiled bark and crushed shells, and no two successive vats ever yielded quite the same shade. Cloth left the bath uneven and alive, marked by the hands that had lowered it in. A metal salt had to go into the bath as well, or the color simply walked away with the first rinse. Dyes made in the laboratory overturned that whole order. They hand you the same shade from one bolt to the next, they hold through washing, and they cost a small fraction of what the old ones did. The gain is real. So is the loss. Where a dyer once read a whole season and a whole harvest in a length of cloth, we read nothing but a repeatable reference. Our closets have gained in steadiness what our eyes have lost in surprise.

units: the text distinguishes three categories of textile materials

text: Three broad families of fiber share the contents of a closet. The first comes off animals. Wool, shorn from a fleece, traps air in its crimp and keeps the cold at a distance. Silk, unwound from a cocoon, gives a smooth, glossy surface. Down, plucked from under the feathers, weighs almost nothing and swells to fill a huge space. The second family grows out of the ground. Cotton, pulled from a boll, soaks up moisture readily. Linen, stripped from a stem, dries fast but creases the moment you sit down. Hemp stands up to hard wear. The third family is made in a plant, where some fibers start as cellulose and others as petroleum, and they can be spun as fine as anyone wants. Each family sets its own rules for washing temperature and for drying. Mix two of them in a single garment and those rules begin to contradict each other.

text: A tailor whose shop stands in one of the older streets received a visit from a customer whose dress had torn at the shoulder on the evening before a ceremony. He studied the tear under a magnifying glass, saw that the weave had given way across a short span, and assured her that the dress could be saved. He began by setting pins around the weakened area so that nothing in it could shift. Then he stretched the cloth over a wooden hoop, to keep the weave from drawing in on itself. From an inside seam he drew a length of thread that matched the color of the dress exactly, and he set about darning the tear one stitch at a time. The whole operation took up much of the evening. When he was done, the damage showed only under a lamp held at a very low angle. The customer went away with the dress she had planned to wear.

units: the heat of the water decides the outcome when washing a wool knit
water that is too hot opens the scales of the fiber

rubbing and wringing by hand cause the same defect as heat

text: Before a wool sweater goes anywhere near the sink, check the temperature of the water, because that is what settles the outcome. Water that runs hot lifts the tiny scales that line each fiber. They catch on one another, the knit mats together, and the sweater comes out smaller for good. Lukewarm water leaves the fiber alone. A mild soap is enough, since anything harsher attacks those same scales. Do not rub the wool and do not wring it out either, because the agitation felts it exactly the way heat does. Press the sweater between two towels instead, then lay it flat to dry. Hung up, it will stretch under its own weight. Brushed leather obeys a different set of rules. Soaking stiffens the surface, so brush it dry with a soft brush, always in one direction. A light surface mark lifts off with an eraser made for the purpose.

text: Inside the sorting warehouse the bags are stacked up to the rafters and the smell of damp cloth catches in your throat. “Ten tons a week come through here, and half of it is worth nothing,” says the woman who runs the place and who has been sorting here for ten years. The volume is not really the problem, she says. The blends are. A shirt that mixes cotton with a plastic fiber cannot be recycled, because there is no way to pull the two apart. So it gets burned, or it gets shipped off somewhere else. Her answer comes in three separate pieces. Make clothes out of one material. Put a readable label on them that states exactly what is inside. And set up repair workshops next to the collection points. Two towns nearby did open one, and what they send for destruction has dropped sharply. She hopes the arrangement gets copied elsewhere.

units: two outdoor garments hang next to each other

text: Two coats hanging from the same rail have almost nothing in common. The first is cut from a thick wool in a deep charcoal, with a surface that catches against the palm like felt. Its seams are doubled, its buttons sewn through four holes, its collar rises to the jaw. It sits heavy on the shoulder, and it will hold up through one cold season after another. The second, a bright blue coated canvas, crushes down inside a fist and folds away into a pocket. Its slick lining slides along the arms, and its zipper runs in a single line from hem to chin. It cuts the wind better than its neighbor, yet it lets the cold straight through the moment the air stops moving. The wool pills in patches, while the coated canvas cracks along the creases. One coat protects you by its weight, the other by its skin.

text: Nothing gives a wardrobe away like the shoulder of a jacket. Stand off to one side and look. If the seam falls in a straight line, someone thought about the garment. If it caves in, the thing was turned out by the yard. You can settle the cut in a second, before your hand ever touches the cloth. The cloth itself reads from the back of the weave, where you find out whether the threads sit packed tight or left slack. The finishing reads in the buttonholes, whose edges should be closed and even. And the upkeep is decided at the counter. A coat with a button you cannot replace and a lining you cannot restitch does not deserve your attachment. A replacement lining lasts as long as the first, provided a seam gives the needle something to grip. We wear what we could never repair, and that helplessness costs us more than we admit.
